title: German musicians, improvisation and syncopating Wagner
summary: German musicians could not follow improvisation, and the band syncopated Tannhauser, which some called sacrilege.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: What about the German musicians. Did they come up to you. There must have been --

Oh, yeah. Yeah, they come up and they couldn't understand it. They couldn't understand what we were doing and why we were doing it. And they didn't know anything about improvising. They were good musicians but they didn't know -- well I'd take a piece, and after the guy's been playing for awhile, I didn't know hardly what he was playing myself.

Especially if they had a solo or something. They'd improvise so much on it that you didn't know what it was. You know, jazz is only the rhythmic -- what I'm trying to say, improvision -- in a rhythmic manner, though. It was syncopated. You see, it's not just improvising, because the white people improvise, but like we say, legato. You write a piece and you have the improvisation on it, but it's not in jazz, you know, in other words, it's not syncopated.
Well that's one thing the blacks had and
especially the Europeans, they'd never heard that before.

You see. So when these fellows would improvise in a rhythmic, syncopated manner, we'd take their own pieces. That's why when you asked me a few minutes ago about "Tannhauser" and all those pieces. We'd first do it like it was. Cause they'd all been trained to -- (sings Tannhauser). And then they turned and come back and, (sings syncopated Tannhauser).
Well that's where the Germans -- and some of them said, "Sacrilege". Cause they couldn't see taking the Wagner damn white man, Wagner, and doing him like that, you see.
